subject: chemistry

moments.title: Fraunhofer lines
moments.body: A self-taught optician finds hundreds of dark lines in the solar spectrum and catalogues them. The lines remain mysterious for 45 years.
moments.takeaway: The Sun's spectrum has hundreds of unexplained dark lines.

moments.title: Bunsen and Kirchhoff
moments.body: Using Bunsen's clean burner and a prism, they show each element has a fingerprint spectrum. They explain Fraunhofer lines as solar atmospheric absorption. Within months they discover caesium and rubidium.
moments.takeaway: Chemistry can now identify elements from their light.

moments.title: Helium in the Sun
moments.body: A yellow line in the solar spectrum, attributed to a new element — helium. It is not found on Earth until 1895 (Ramsay).
moments.takeaway: An element is discovered on the Sun before being found on Earth.

moments.title: Raman spectroscopy
moments.body: Raman discovers that scattered light has shifted frequencies revealing vibrational modes. He wins the 1930 Nobel — the first Asian to win a science Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Inelastic light scattering becomes a workhorse of molecular spectroscopy.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Spectroscopy (UV-Vis, IR, Raman, NMR, MS) is the chemist's primary characterisation toolkit. Modern instruments are 1000x more sensitive than 1960s versions.
now.open_questions: Can single-molecule spectroscopy become routine? Can we identify protein states in vivo?

reflection: Bunsen's burner, invented for clean spectroscopy, became the most iconic apparatus in school chemistry. How does pure research equipment become pedagogy?
